Creating a DNS itself server is relatively simple. There are plenty of free Linux/Unix options, and even the basic windows server versions come with the capability.

The real challenge is getting people to use it at scale. Beyond even spreading word to people about it and having them modify settings away from the automatic DNS they tend to get from the ISP. Most businesses for instance use a "local" DNS server that only contains records of computer and resources in that company's network. Anything request not contained in its records is "forwarded" to an Internet DNS such as the Google/cloudflare/ISP run servers.

This separation of work is critical so no one DNS is overwhelmed with having to track the entire internet. Mechanically speaking these DNS server are all the same. Anything that one DNS server doesn't know goes up chain to another until one gives an answer.

So even if you setup an independent DNS server (and there are many already) for a limited set of DNS records such as "voat" it would still have to refer up to other public DNS as no one server can actually handle all records of the internet alone. Forwarding isn't enough though as a DDOS can occur accidentally through sheer volume of requests from even legitimate users. Thus you use multiple DNS servers with copies or segments of your list of records that can share the load but still respond to one IP which is what round Robin actually is.

How many servers you need becomes a function of how many people use your DNS service over how big a set of DNS records you host. Big registrars may LOOK like one or two IPs but are serviced by hundreds or thousands of servers in order to cache something as big as the general internet. Ergo why only giant companies tend to do it and share records automatically.

Thus if you only service a small subset of DNS records for a limited number of sites and forward the rest you still need at least a dozen or more DNS setup to share the burden to prevent effectively being DDOS'ed by legitimate traffic.
